skills.name: Location of firms: site choice, clusters and policy

note.text: Location chooses a site for an activity; localisation describes concentration of related activities in an area. A cluster may support skills, suppliers and shared services, but congestion, competition for resources or environmental pressures can offset benefits. Public authorities may influence location through infrastructure or incentives. An incentive is one factor, not proof of an efficient or suitable site. Compare complete relevant costs and essential constraints; some social and environmental effects cannot be reduced to the few amounts in a classroom table.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to compare complete site evidence and distinguish firm location from industrial concentration. Builds on: input, market, labour and infrastructure factors. Leads to: later production, cost and market analysis using evidence rather than one-factor rules.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional repair cluster near Bamenda offers access to suppliers and trained workers, but its crowded access road may delay deliveries. A proposed alternative has lower rent yet less reliable services. The case asks pupils to compare stated evidence and identify missing facts, without recommending a real place or claiming a current government incentive.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Use a comparison sheet: rent, inward transport, outward delivery, essential services, workforce and effects on others. Sum only comparable monetary items and avoid counting the same cost twice. State a provisional choice with a reason and a limitation. A cheapest stated total is not enough if the site fails an essential requirement.

key_words.meaning: concentration of related industrial activities in an area
an advantage from nearby related firms, skills or suppliers
a policy measure intended to attract or support activity in a place
weighing relevant costs and constraints rather than a single attractive feature

mistake.wrong: Localisation means only one firm choosing any isolated site.
mistake.right: localisation: concentration of related industrial activities in an area.
mistake.why: The term concerns a concentration of activities, not just an individual location.

worked_example.problem: A fictional site has rent {3000}, input transport {2000} and delivery {1000}; the alternative’s comparable total is {7500} CFA francs. Compare the stated totals.
steps: Check missing costs and essential services before deciding.
worked_example.answer: The first site costs {7500-3000-2000-1000} CFA francs less on the stated items.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: localisation: concentration of related industrial activities in an area.
cluster benefit: an advantage from nearby related firms, skills or suppliers.
location incentive: a policy measure intended to attract or support activity in a place.
complete site comparison: weighing relevant costs and constraints rather than a single attractive feature.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: Several related workshops operate near common specialist suppliers.
Shared access to a specialist input service benefits several workshops.
A hypothetical authority offers support that changes a site’s stated costs.
The pupil compares transport and reliability as well as rent.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: localisation: The term concerns a concentration of activities, not just an individual location.
cluster benefit: Benefits must be weighed against crowding and competing resource demands.
location incentive: Service, demand and operating constraints remain even if one cost is reduced.
complete site comparison: Other costs and essential conditions can overturn a rent-only ranking.

questions.prompt: Invented monthly cost record: Site A has rent {arent}, input transport {ain} and outward delivery {aout}; Site B’s complete comparable total is {btotal}, all in CFA francs. How much lower is A’s stated total than B’s?

misconceptions.explain: That omits A’s input and outward transport costs.
That is A’s total, not its saving relative to B.

solution: This compares only the stated costs; check service reliability and other constraints separately.
